extracted.intended_audience: legislators, statesmen, political reformers, and readers interested in principles of prudent government and reform (late-18th-century context)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative principles for lawmakers and statesmen about how to reform institutions and manage public policy without destroying property, stability, or justice. Emphasizes gradualism, respect for property, prudence, and use of existing institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for property and prescription
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliaments have no right to violate property, to overrule prescription, or to force a currency of their own fiction in the place of that which is real.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative action should not arbitrarily confiscate or override long-established property rights and legal prescriptions; destroying property undermines stability and is tantamount to tyranny. Beware legislation that treats prescription as inapplicable to assemblies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislature's role — security not destruction of property
rubrics_metrics.description: A legislative assembly of a free nation should sit for the security, not for the destruction of property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws and parliamentary acts ought to promote the stability and circulation of property rather than destroy rules and maxims that give property security; measures that systematically impair property or its instruments are illegitimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against fanaticism and proselytism
rubrics_metrics.description: The spirit of atheistical fanaticism, inspired by numerous writings and sermons, fills the populace with atrocity of mind, superseding common feelings and morality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy-makers should be alert to epidemical fanaticism and organized proselytism (societies caballing and corresponding) that destabilize society; such movements can erode morality and property norms and spread internationally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware international spread of revolutionary contagion
rubrics_metrics.description: Radical schemes aim at destroying prosperous states (e.g., the republic of Berne) and seek correspondences and leagues abroad to propagate discontent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Governments should recognize and resist cross-border propagation of revolutionary doctrines and domestic sympathizers who recommend foreign examples; monitor and counteract organized efforts to export instability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not adopt confiscation as state policy
rubrics_metrics.description: It is dangerous if a state considers it policy to seek resources in confiscations of any kind or to regard some citizens as proper prey for confiscation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confiscation as a policy instrument breeds insecurity, invites arbitrary seizures of property, and sets a precedent likely to be abused against other classes; avoid turning confiscation into a revenue source or political tool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage public debt to avoid empowering dangerous interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive public debts, at first a security, in excess become means of subversion — creating a discontented moneyed interest seeking security in new energetic governments derived from contempt of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Governments should be cautious about over-indebtedness; if debts force heavy impositions they become odious, but if left unpaid they empower an angry moneyed class that may favor new, unjust regimes — fiscal policy affects political stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain tenacity for justice and tenderness for property during change
rubrics_metrics.description: In all mutations the circumstance most likely to blunt mischief is that people remain tenacious of justice and tender of property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During reforms or upheavals, adherence to justice and respect for property rights mitigates harm; cultivate civic commitments to these principles to reduce revolutionary damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority of justice as standing policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice is itself the great standing policy of civil society; departures from it are suspect of being no policy at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy decisions should be judged first by their justice; purported policy goals do not justify gross injustices — the long-term prudence of measures depends on their justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid arbitrary degradation and expulsion of citizens
rubrics_metrics.description: It is unjust for a legislature, by an arbitrary act, to degrade people from their state and condition, stigmatize them with shame, expel them from habitations, or confiscate their goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws that suddenly strip people of social status, property, or residence without just cause are morally and politically indefensible — reform must not operate by caprice or punitive humiliation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider systemic interdependencies before total abolition
rubrics_metrics.description: When institutions have cast deep roots and are interwoven with many valuable things, their total abolition cannot be done without notably impairing the others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how established institutions link with other social goods; prefer reforms that preserve useful components rather than wholesale destruction, since destruction can cause collateral loss of valuable functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve and improve existing materials — 'Spartam nactus es; hanc exorna.'
rubrics_metrics.description: A good patriot and true politician always considers how to make the most of the existing materials of his country; a disposition to preserve and an ability to improve is the standard of a statesman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reformers should adapt and embellish current institutions rather than treating the society as a blank slate; incremental improvement is preferable to radical reinvention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use institutional resources rather than destroying them (monastic example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Monastic institutions contained revenues, disciplined men dedicated to public purposes, and perennial corporate fortunes suited to long views; these were usable powers for public benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than selling or destroying institutions with public functions, consider repurposing their resources and human capital for public ends; public direction of corporate property can yield sustained benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer tolerable superstitions that build over those that demolish
rubrics_metrics.description: Superstition may be prejudicial in excess, but some forms (that build, adorn, endow) are more tolerable than those that demolish or plunder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing which errors or enthusiasms to remedy, prioritize tolerating those that contribute cultural or social goods rather than eliminating all forms of superstition reflexively; weigh moral costs against social functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare the social effects of old possessors vs purchasers
rubrics_metrics.description: Before violent revolutions in property, have reasonable assurance that purchasers of confiscated property will be more laborious, virtuous, sober, and better for laborers than the old possessors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economic and social consequences of transferring property matter: examine whether new owners will distribute surplus product more beneficially and not consume or extort more than predecessors; do not assume transfer improves public good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize corporate bodies as amenable to public direction
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporate bodies are more susceptible of a public direction, in the use of their property and in regulating modes and habits of life, than private citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead of abolishing corporate institutions, consider using state power to direct or reform their administration to achieve public aims while preserving continuity and institutional advantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value tenure tied to duty and stewardship
rubrics_metrics.description: Estates passing through persons whose title involves piety, morals, and learning and the performance of duties may provide renovation and support to families and dignity to the lowly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hold that property arranged with duties attached can foster stewardship, charity, and decorous behavior; tenure linked to responsibilities can be preferable to purely private, discretionary ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor slow, tested, and experiential reform over rapid upheaval
rubrics_metrics.description: Proceed by slow but well-sustained progress; the effect of each step is watched, the success of the first gives light to the second; time is among the assistants of good method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement reforms incrementally, observe outcomes, adapt subsequent measures based on experience, and allow time for social minds to coalesce — patience and circumspection are virtues in public change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislator's temperament — sensibility, love of kind, and fear of himself
rubrics_metrics.description: The true lawgiver ought to have a heart full of sensibility; he ought to love and respect his kind, and to fear himself; movements ought to be deliberate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lawmakers should be humane and self-aware, tempering visionary zeal with compassion and caution; moral character and humility are essential qualifications for sound legislation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy requires prescription or necessity for revolutionary authority
rubrics_metrics.description: A new, experimental government derived from no law and no necessity, which originated in vices and sinister practices, lacks the prescription that confers legitimacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political authority established by sudden revolution must still demonstrate justifying necessity or acquire legitimacy through time and usage; be cautious in recognizing powers without established sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply tested arts to public good; avoid untried speculations
rubrics_metrics.description: Everything done to obtain and keep power follows common arts, precedents of ambition; but in regulations relative to the public good they commit to the mercy of untried speculations with no experience to prove benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing public policy favor methods grounded in experience and precedent rather than theoretical novelties; do not entrust fundamental public interests to speculative schemes lacking empirical support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confront and wrestle with difficulty to produce durable solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Difficulty obliges an intimate acquaintance with the object and compels consideration in all its relations; to proceed with a presiding principle and prolific energy is the criterion of profound wisdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective polity requires confronting hard problems rather than eliding them; durable reforms come from engagement with complexity and the disciplined application of principles over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid confusing destruction with skillful reform
rubrics_metrics.description: Destroying and pulling down is not skill; mobs can destroy as well as assemblies. Rage will pull down more in half an hour than prudence can build in a hundred years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reformers should not equate obliteration with progress; building stable institutions requires skill, foresight, and sustained effort — value constructive composition over mere negation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for composition and reconciliation rather than crude simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Preserve useful parts of an old establishment and fit superadded reforms to what is retained; the excellence is in composition — uniting anomalies and contending principles into a consistent whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design reforms that reconcile competing interests, compensate harms, and balance trade-offs; prefer complex, composed solutions that integrate multiple concerns rather than simplistic 'all or nothing' fixes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware reformers who only detest and display faults
rubrics_metrics.description: Those habitually employed in finding and displaying faults are unqualified for reformation because their minds lack patterns of the fair and good; by hating vices too much they come to love men too little.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select reformers and advisors who can imagine and implement positive alternatives, not only criticize; seek policymakers who understand and value existing good as well as detect faults.
